title: Phileas Foggarty and the Upside-Down Seeds
markdown:
Professor Phileas Foggarty adjusted his spectacles and a few metal shavings fell onto the workbench. He stood in his garden patch among sunflowers taller than houses and the strong, sweet smell of plump tomatoes. This was not only a garden. It was the outdoor half of his inventing life. Phileas was a goat with ideas so large they sometimes shouldered the small details out of the way.

“Otis, my good friend,” he called, voice bright as a newly cut gear. “Look at this. The best gardening invention ever.”

Otis the pigeon blinked his dark, careful eyes. He was a quiet observer, a contrast to the energetic goat, and he often sat on a high dusty shelf while machines came to life. The garden around them hummed with ordinary work. Mrs. Higgins next door, in a flowery hat, polished her trowel until it shone. Mr. Fitzwilliam, whose voice rumbled like his prize potatoes, hummed a tune as he tied up beans. Little Lily, pigtails bouncing, giggled after a butterfly through the marigolds. It was a peaceful picture, and it did not appear to need improving.

Phileas was always thinking about the extraordinary. He patted a collection of shiny brass gears, spinning wheels, and several small tin funnels. “No more bending. No more reaching. Imagine, Otis, a garden that looks after itself.”

He waved a hoof in a grand circle.

Otis cooed softly. It might have meant, That sounds interesting. It might have meant, Are you sure.

“It works simply,” Phileas explained. “A water tank uses gravity, which is a clever idea, and timed parts plant the seeds just so and give each one the right drink. Music for the garden.”

The machine shone. Near the seed spout sat a cherry-red spring, coiled like a tiny ladybird that had ideas of its own.

Phileas flipped the big switch. The machine sprang into clicks and whirs and a soft hiss. Gears turned. Levers nodded. Tiny seeds dropped into neat rows. A fine mist found each one. Phileas’s chest puffed.

“Wonderful. Perfect. Every seed placed just right. Every seed watered. People will want to visit.”

Otis tilted his head. He had been watching the neighbours’ quiet work, and he had been watching the seeds. Something about the seeds made his pigeon mind feel uneasy, the way a picture frame feels when it is a degree off.

“Professor,” he chirped, a soft sound that cut through the fading whir.

“Yes, yes. Amazed, are you? It happens.”

“No, Professor.” Otis hopped closer. His claws tapped the workbench. “All the seeds are upside down.”

Phileas scoffed. “Impossible. My plans are perfect. A pigeon can be confused by greatness.”

He looked at the neat rows in the damp earth.

Then he saw it.

Every seed sat with its pointy end toward the soil and its root-seeking end aimed at the sky. They were a tiny army in perfect lines, and they were completely, politely wrong.

A tremble ran through Phileas’s whiskers. The garden’s ordinary sounds, which had felt so comforting, now seemed to go on being content without him. His loud voice thinned to a question.

“But how? The dispenser should have put them the right way.”

Otis, who had watched the parts more keenly than the speech, hopped onto the bench and nudged the cherry-red spring with his beak.

“This spring,” he said, calm as a well-tied bean. “It gives the last push, from the wrong side. If it were turned around, the heavier end would land down, ready to grow.”

Phileas stared. One small red spring. He had been so busy with gears and the grand idea of changing gardening that he had forgotten how a seed behaves. It was like building a tower by admiring the weathercock and ignoring the first brick.

A faint blush warmed his goat cheeks. He reached out and turned the spring. It settled with a small ping.

He flipped the switch again. The machine whirred. The water misted. This time the seeds dropped with their root-seeking ends toward the sky and their heavier ends into the nourishing earth, which was, as it happened, the right kind of upside down.

Phileas let out a long breath, relief mixed with a surprised sort of delight. Otis landed on his shoulder and offered a comforting coo. Mrs. Higgins’s trowel flashed once in the sun. Lily’s butterfly moved on, unimpressed by invention.

The tomatoes still smelled sweet and earthy. Phileas watched the perfectly planted row, and the cherry-red spring, now facing the proper way, caught the light like a ladybird that had decided to stay.
characters: Phileas Foggarty (an inventive goat inventor), Otis (a pigeon friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
